xmldoc.short_description: Build an nflow model with the scripted API, step by step.

syntax.syntax_item: Guide: new_system, add_block, add_line, set_param, sim, save_system.

description.p: This guide teaches how to build a complete nflow model from the Nelson command line, without the editor. We start from the smallest model that runs, explain every line, then grow it into a realistic signal model and a physical (acausal) circuit. If you have not seen nflow before, read it top to bottom; if you only need a reminder, jump to the examples.
An nflow model is a set of blocks (boxes that produce or transform values) joined by wires. You build one in the same five moves every time:

ol.li: Wire the blocks together with add_line.
Configure the run (duration, step, solver) with set_param.
Run or save with sim, save_system, and tidy the picture with nflow_layout.

description.p: There are two families of model. A causal (signal) model flows in one direction: a value leaves an output port, travels along a wire, and arrives at an input port, like the blocks of a flowchart. A physical (acausal) model instead describes real components (resistors, masses, thermal bodies) whose pins are tied together into nodes, with no fixed direction of flow. We build a causal model first, then a physical one.

p.b: Step 1: the smallest model that runs

description.p: Before anything realistic, here is the whole workflow in four blocks of code: a constant value shown on a scope. Read the comments, then run it.

Line by line: new_system opens an empty model named 'first'. Each add_block takes a library path ('nflow/<library>/<type>', telling nflow which kind of block to create) and a destination ('first/Name', where Name is how you will refer to that block). Optional name/value pairs set parameters, so 'Value', 1 makes the constant equal to 1. add_line draws the wire: 'C/1' is output port 1 of block C, 'Scope/1' is input port 1 of block Scope. set_param says how long to run. bdclose discards the in-memory model at the end so the example leaves nothing behind.

Now the same recipe with three blocks that actually compute something: a sine source, a gain that multiplies by 2, and a scope. The new ideas are that a block can transform its input (the gain), and that you can chain several wires. We also lay the diagram out and save it to a file, then run it from that file.

Two practices are worth keeping. We call nflow_layout so the auto-placed blocks are spread into a readable left-to-right diagram instead of stacked. And we write the file under tempdir (a scratch folder), never into your project, so the example is self-contained.

p.b: Wiring: numbered ports vs named pins

description.p: An add_line endpoint is written 'Block/port'. The text after the slash decides what kind of connection you are making, and this is the single most important rule to understand:

ul.li: A number, such as 'Src/1', means a signal port: output port 1 on the source side, input port 1 on the target side. Numbering is 1-based (the first port is 1, not 0). Signal wires have a direction: value flows from the output to the input.
A name, such as 'R1/p' or 'M1/flange', means a physical pin of an acausal block. Physical joints have no direction; they tie two pins into one node.

description.p: Both ends of one add_line must be the same kind. Joining 'A/1' (a number) to 'B/p' (a name) is an error, because a signal wire and a physical joint are different things.

p.b: Step 3: a physical (acausal) model: series RLC

description.p: Physical models look different because you wire real components, not signals. A few points explain how they work:

ul.li: A pin carries two quantities at once: an across variable (voltage, temperature, position) and a through variable (current, heat flow, force). When you join pins, nflow balances both at that point. That is what acausal means: you state what is connected, and the solver works out the directions.

Joining two pins makes one node. To tie three or more pins to the same node (a single electrical junction, mechanical joint, or thermal point), make successive add_line calls that share a pin: they merge into one node. In the example, the two calls on 'C1/p' put L1.n, C1.p and VS.p on one node.
An electrical circuit needs a Ground on every reference node, or the equations have no unique solution. We add two grounds and wire their 'p' pins.

A sensor is a bridge between the two worlds: it has physical pins (wired with named add_line) and one numbered signal output (wired with a numbered add_line to the scope). So 'VS/p' and 'VS/n' join the circuit, while 'VS/1' carries the measured voltage out as a signal.
Every physical model uses the 'dae' solver: set_param(model, 'Solver', 'dae').

description.p: The example below builds a series RLC circuit: a constant voltage source drives a resistor, inductor and capacitor in series back to ground, and a voltage sensor reads the capacitor voltage onto a scope.

p.b: Choosing the solver and the step

description.p: Set the run with set_param: StopTime (how many seconds), SampleTime (the base step), and Solver. Causal models use 'discrete' (the default fixed-step engine), 'ode4' (fixed-step Runge-Kutta, more accurate) or 'ode45' (adaptive step). Physical models require 'dae'. See nflow_solvers for the full list and the tolerances.

ul.li: Mixing a numbered port and a named pin in one add_line: pick one kind for both ends.
Forgetting a Ground on a physical reference node: the solver reports a singular system.
Leaving the solver on the default for a physical model: set 'dae'.
Expecting a signal input to stay unconnected: every input port a block needs must be wired.
Confusing the API and the file: add_line uses 1-based port numbers, while the saved .nflow stores 0-based indices (see nflow_model_format).

example_item.example_item_description: Step 1: the smallest model that runs, a constant shown on a scope.
example_item.example_item_data: new_system('first'); % create an empty model add_block('nflow/source/constant', 'first/C', 'Value', 1); % a block named C add_block('nflow/sink/scope', 'first/Scope'); % a scope named Scope add_line('first', 'C/1', 'Scope/1'); % wire C output 1 -> Scope input 1 set_param('first', 'StopTime', 5); % run for 5 seconds bdclose('first'); % discard the in-memory model

example_item.example_item_description: Step 2: a signal model (sine -> gain -> scope); lay it out, save to tempdir, then simulate from the file.
Step 3: a physical series RLC; named pins joined with add_line, shared pins merge into one node, solver 'dae'.
